archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, defense-led)
archetype.definition: A team climbing out of back-to-back 3-14 seasons that now competes weekly behind a sturdy line and a better defense, but lacks a passing game that can finish drives or games.

report.headline: Competitive 0-4: real defensive progress, but the passing game can't move chains
report.take:
The 0-4 record understates what has changed in Tennessee. The last two seasons were 3-14 disasters, with net EPA ranking 27th and then 31st and more than 27 points allowed per game both years. This team has lost by 13, 4, 5 and 6, allows 20.8 points per game (9th), and has lifted its net EPA from -0.252 last year to -0.112. That is still 28th, so this is not a good team yet, but it is a much harder out than the 2025 version.

The defining trait is a run-first offense that can't sustain anything. Tennessee passes less than any team relative to situation (pass rate over expected -10.5, 32nd), and the line has earned that trust: a 5th-ranked stuff rate, a 12th-ranked rushing EPA, and the 7th-lowest pressure rate allowed. The trouble is everything that has to happen through the air. Pass EPA ranks 25th, Cam Ward is averaging about 181 passing yards a game, and the offense is last in yards (261.8) and 31st in scoring. The strangest number explains the rest: the most run-heavy team in football also has the league's lowest time of possession (24.3 minutes). A ground game should eat clock, so that only happens when drives keep dying after a few plays. Add special teams that are dead last at -5.27 EPA per game, roughly the size of the margin in three of the four losses, and a 2-to-5 takeaway-giveaway split, and you get a team that keeps games close and keeps losing them.

The 9th-ranked scoring defense is softer than it looks. It is genuinely good against the run, on early downs and on third down, and it tackles well. But it ranks 27th in pass EPA allowed and 31st on deep throws, and 22nd in red-zone touchdown rate. Two of its four opponents, Philadelphia (29th) and the Giants (23rd), rank in the bottom third offensively today. When Baltimore's 4th-ranked offense showed up, it threw for 285 yards. The -1.39 wins over expected says some bad luck is baked into 0-4, so this plays more like a 1-3 team than a winless one, but the efficiency numbers don't hide a secret contender.

Where it goes from here depends on the interior line holding together and on Ward giving the offense a second dimension. Both guards who started early, Fernando Carmona and Jackson Slater, went on IR before Week 4, and that game produced the worst rushing EPA of the year (-5.2). Their estimated return is around Nov. 1. The schedule offers real chances: two games each against Indianapolis and Houston, plus Washington and Pittsburgh. A four- or five-win season with clear progress is the realistic shape. Anything more needs the passing game to stop killing drives.

strengths.title: A line that holds up both ways
strengths.body: Tennessee allows pressure on just 15.4% of dropbacks and gets stuffed on only 16% of runs, both top-seven marks, so the run-heavy identity has a foundation rather than being stubbornness. Rushing EPA ranks 12th even though the offense around it is bottom-five. The catch is depth: both guards are on IR until roughly Nov. 1, and the first game without them was the worst rushing day of the season.

strengths.title: Run defense and standard-down discipline
strengths.body: The defense ranks 10th in success rate allowed and 10th on third down, and misses tackles less often than all but five teams. That keeps offenses behind the chains and makes the run an unattractive option for opponents. It is a meaningful step from last season's 28th-ranked defensive EPA, and sound tackling is the kind of skill that tends to hold up.

strengths.title: Clean, aggressive game management
strengths.body: Only two teams commit fewer penalties, and Tennessee goes for it on fourth down more readily than any team in the league. For an offense that struggles to string plays together, not giving away yards and keeping possessions alive is how it manufactures points. Neither habit depends on luck, so both should carry forward.

concerns.title: The passing game can't sustain drives
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 25th and the offense is last in yards. The league-low time of possession, despite the league's most run-heavy approach, shows that drives are ending quickly. That is the real flaw, not a cost of the system. Passing yards have climbed each week since the opener (140 to 222), which is the thread to watch, but until third-and-medium becomes manageable the offense will live below 20 points.

concerns.title: Deep balls beat this defense
concerns.body: Tennessee is 31st in EPA allowed on deep throws and 27th in explosive pass rate, while the pressure rate (23rd) isn't heating up quarterbacks enough to cover for it. With only two takeaways, the secondary isn't trading big plays for turnovers either. A softer early schedule muted the damage, and the back half has Dallas, Detroit, Cincinnati and Jacksonville twice.

concerns.title: Special teams are losing games
concerns.body: At -5.27 EPA per game, Tennessee has the worst special teams in the league, a deficit close to the final margin in the 4-, 5- and 6-point losses. Special-teams performance is volatile week to week and usually drifts back toward average, so some of this should correct. That correction is a big part of why more wins should come.

trend.note: After the 13-point opening loss, every game has been decided by six or fewer, and passing yards have risen in each of the last three weeks. The run game has gone the other way, from +3.9 rushing EPA against Philadelphia to -5.2 at Baltimore, the first game after both guards went on IR.

nextGame.headline: Two winless teams, but the line prices them as different tiers
nextGame.body:
Houston is a mirror image of Tennessee. It can pass a little, ranking 15th in pass EPA, but it can't run at all: 2.96 yards per carry and rushing EPA 30th. Tennessee's defense is solid against the run and leaky deep, so this game turns on whether C.J. Stroud gets enough time for downfield shots. On the other side, Houston's defense has the league's 2nd-best sack rate and 4th-best success rate allowed, but it gives up the 29th-worst deep-ball EPA. Those numbers invite exactly the shot plays Tennessee's offense has been unable to hit.

Availability matters on both sides. Tennessee plays its second straight game without guards Carmona and Slater, which tests the line's run blocking and its ability to handle Houston's pass rush. Houston is without linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair (92% of snaps), and Kenneth Murray Jr. (82%) is questionable with a head injury. That leaves the second level thin against a team running the ball 54 times through Tony Pollard alone. Tank Dell is expected to open his practice window, which suggests he isn't a factor yet.

keyMatchups.title: Pollard vs. a linebacker-depleted front
keyMatchups.body: Houston's run defense ranks 12th in EPA, but losing its every-down linebacker and possibly a second one weakens it right where Tennessee attacks. Tennessee's interior is patched too, after posting -5.2 rushing EPA last week. Whichever side's replacements hold up decides whether Tennessee can play its preferred low-possession game.

keyMatchups.title: Houston's sack rush vs. Ward
keyMatchups.body: Houston gets sacks on 8.7% of dropbacks, 2nd in the league, while Tennessee has kept Ward clean with the 9th-best sack rate allowed. With two guards out, interior pressure is the obvious stress point. Sacks would turn Tennessee's already short drives into punts.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots, both directions
keyMatchups.body: Both defenses are bottom-four against deep throws, and both have little room for error underneath. Houston's passing game is the more functional of the two, which is the main reason it should have an edge. Still, Carnell Tate's 32 targets show where Ward will look when he takes his shots.

nextGame.watch: Whether the reshuffled interior line can get Pollard above his 3.74 yards per carry against a Houston front missing Al-Shaair. That decides whether Tennessee can shorten the game.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts of this team that should last are the line (once the guards return around Nov. 1), the run defense and the discipline. The parts that should improve are special teams, which can hardly be worse than -5.27 EPA a game, and close-game luck, after an 0-3 record in one-score games. The parts that may get worse are the pass defense's results. The back half brings Dallas (2nd offense), Detroit (6th), Cincinnati (10th) and Jacksonville twice (7th), and those offenses will test a secondary that has been beaten deep all year. Expect points allowed to drift up from 20.8 even if the underlying defense stays the same.

The winnable stretch is concentrated: Houston twice, Indianapolis twice, Washington and Pittsburgh are all opponents ranked 20th or worse on offense or with losing records. A team that loses by single digits should steal three to five of those. The ceiling is set by the passing game. Unless Ward's efficiency climbs out of the bottom eight, this offense lives in the mid-to-high teens and can't overcome a bad special-teams day or a turnover.
swingFactors: Guards Carmona and Slater returning around Nov. 1
Ward's passing efficiency on third down and deep shots

bets.reason: These are near-identical teams: point differential per game is -7.0 vs. -6.3 and net EPA is -0.112 vs. -0.094. Yet Houston is laying a full touchdown on the road while 0-4 against the spread and missing its top linebacker. Tennessee lost by 4 and 6 when getting 7 or more against Philadelphia and Baltimore.

At +275 the price implies roughly a 27% chance, which is low for a home team whose efficiency is close to its opponent's. Tennessee's league-worst special teams and weak passing game keep this a small play rather than a strong one.

confidence.note: Four games, two starting guards newly on IR, and special-teams numbers that are noisy at this sample size.
